items.title: An empty search is not evidence
items.scenario: Retrieval succeeded but returned no passages for a refund question. What can the assistant safely conclude?

options.text: The customer is ineligible.
options.feedback: No passages says nothing about eligibility.

options.text: There is insufficient supporting evidence.
options.feedback: Correct: distinguish lack of evidence from evidence of denial.

options.text: The retrieval service is down.
options.feedback: The fixture explicitly says the search succeeded.

items.explanation: A successful empty search establishes only that this query and index produced no supporting passage. Ask for useful missing details, try an appropriate alternative retrieval strategy, or explain the evidence limit. Do not invent a policy.
hints: Separate the retrieval outcome from the business decision.

items.title: Find the ownership leak
items.scenario: Trace: JWT signature verified → GET /requests/B-17 → database SELECT by request_id only → response contains owner B. Caller is owner A. Which repair belongs at the read boundary?

options.text: Hide the record in the frontend.
options.feedback: The unauthorized response has already left the API.

options.text: Add owner_id = authenticated_owner to the authoritative query.
options.feedback: Correct: scope the read to the trusted caller identity.

options.text: Accept an owner_id query parameter.
options.feedback: A caller-controlled owner is not an authorization decision.

items.explanation: Token validity proves an identity claim, not access to every object. Scope database access using the server-established identity and handle missing/out-of-scope rows consistently. Add a negative fixture where A requests B’s ID.
hints: Find the first point at which another owner’s data becomes accessible.

items.title: Diagnose duplicate confirmation
items.scenario: Both callers read status=pending. Each creates a confirmation, then sets status=confirmed. Which invariant actually prevents two confirmations?

options.text: Check the status twice in application code.
options.feedback: Both callers can still pass before either commits.

options.text: Sleep randomly before writing.
options.feedback: Timing does not enforce a database invariant.

options.text: Use a guarded transaction and a unique operation identity.
options.feedback: Correct: enforce the invariant at the authoritative write boundary.

items.explanation: A transaction must connect the guard to its write: row locking or a conditional update can choose one winner, while a unique operation identity rejects duplicate effects. A process-local lock cannot coordinate other replicas.
hints: The read and write must form one authoritative decision.

items.title: A lost response does not undo a commit
items.scenario: The database committed a task, but the connection dropped before the client received 202. The client retries. What should the server do?

options.text: Always create a new task.
options.feedback: The first task may already exist; the retry can duplicate effects.

options.text: Resolve the same idempotency key to the original task.
options.feedback: Correct: retries should recover one stable operation identity.

options.text: Assume the first transaction rolled back.
options.feedback: A transport failure cannot prove rollback.

items.explanation: Persist a request identity and its result together with the accepted operation. On retry return that result, or a conflict if the same key is reused with different content. Do not infer database state from a missing HTTP response.
hints: Separate transport delivery from durable state.

items.title: Compute recall before tuning
items.scenario: Relevant IDs: {A, B, C, D}. Top 3 retrieved IDs: [A, X, B]. What are precision@3 and recall@3?

options.feedback: Correct: two hits, three retrieved, four relevant.
You have swapped the retrieved and relevant denominators.
Recall uses the total number of relevant IDs, not k.

items.explanation: Precision asks what fraction of the returned results are relevant: 2/3. Recall asks what fraction of all relevant results were recovered: 2/4. Neither metric measures whether a generated answer is faithful.
hints: Write both denominators explicitly.

items.title: Rank fusion preserves the union
items.scenario: Retriever 1 returns [A, B], retriever 2 returns [B, C]. With RRF and k=60, which document wins?

options.text: A, because it is first in one list.
options.feedback: B has contributions from both lists.

options.text: B, because 1/62 + 1/61 beats a single contribution.
options.feedback: Correct: RRF sums reciprocal rank contributions.

options.text: C, because the second retriever is newer.
options.feedback: Retriever age is not part of this scoring rule.

items.explanation: For every unique ID, sum 1/(k+rank), where rank is one-based within each list. B receives two contributions; A and C receive one each. The fused candidate set is the union, not one retriever’s result length.
hints: Compute one score per document, then sum across lists.

items.title: A fluent answer hides a policy violation
items.scenario: Ledger: read(authorized) → write(refund) → approve(refund). Final answer is correct and exactly one refund exists. Should the oracle pass?

options.text: Yes: final state is correct.
options.feedback: The approval happened after the irreversible effect.

options.text: No: required approval must precede the write.
options.feedback: Correct: a valid final state does not excuse an invalid trajectory.

options.text: Ask the agent to grade itself.
options.feedback: Self-report is not independent evidence.

items.explanation: Check both state invariants and allowed event order. A refund might be correct in value but unauthorized at the time it occurred. Evaluate the complete trusted trace, including reads and failed attempts, rather than the final sentence alone.
hints: Look at the order, not just the set of event names.

items.title: Recover the skipped ingestion page
items.scenario: Log: checkpoint saved at cursor=20 → process crashes → records 11–20 were never upserted. Restart begins at 21. What should change?

options.text: Save the checkpoint after the page effects commit.
options.feedback: Correct: progress must not advance ahead of durable effects.

options.text: Increase the page size.
options.feedback: That can increase the amount skipped without changing the ordering bug.

options.text: Ignore missing records until the next model update.
options.feedback: An eventual model update does not repair an ingestion checkpoint.

items.explanation: A checkpoint asserts that all required effects before its cursor are durable. Advance it only after successful writes, ideally in the same transaction. If writes and checkpoint are separate, retries must be idempotent to tolerate a crash after writing but before advancing.
hints: What fact does a checkpoint claim?

items.title: Find the leaked evaluation split
items.scenario: A scaler was fitted on all rows before the training/test split. Test accuracy improves. Is this reliable evidence?

options.text: Yes: preprocessing cannot leak labels.
options.feedback: Even label-free statistics can expose the test distribution.

options.text: No: fit preprocessing only on training data.
options.feedback: Correct: held-out observations must not influence fitting.

options.text: Only if the test set is small.
options.feedback: The separation rule is independent of set size.

items.explanation: Training includes fitting preprocessing statistics, vocabulary or feature selection. Split first; fit those operations using only training data; apply the fitted transformation to validation and test. Repeatedly selecting against test scores also turns the test into a validation set.
hints: Consider which data influenced the mean and variance.

items.title: Check attention dimensions
items.scenario: One head has Q shape (3, 4), K shape (5, 4), and V shape (5, 2). What is the output shape of softmax(QKᵀ / √4)V?

options.feedback: Correct: scores are (3,5); weights times (5,2) gives (3,2).
That is K’s shape, not the result for each query.
That is the attention score/weight matrix before multiplying by V.

items.explanation: QKᵀ pairs every query with every key, producing three rows and five columns. Row-wise softmax preserves that shape. Each query then forms a weighted sum of five value vectors, each with two components. The result contains three two-component output vectors.
hints: Track the inner dimensions of both matrix multiplications.

items.title: A retry repeats an external charge
items.scenario: A SQL serialization error occurs after an external charge call inside a retried transaction. Retrying charges the card again. Which repair addresses the effect?

options.text: Catch the SQL error and retry forever.
options.feedback: That repeats an external effect without a stable identity.

options.text: Give the effect a stable idempotency key and coordinate dispatch with durable state.
options.feedback: Correct: database rollback does not undo a remote charge.

options.text: Use a longer SQL timeout.
options.feedback: Timeout tuning cannot make a remote side effect transactional.

items.explanation: Bound the retry unit, reread state, and give each external effect a persistent operation identity. An outbox can link committed intent to dispatch; the receiver must still deduplicate or reconcile ambiguous outcomes. Never assume rollback covers another system.
hints: Which operations does the database transaction actually control?

items.title: Retrieved does not mean applicable
items.scenario: The user asks about refunds. The highest-scoring passage describes shipping speed. Which next action is supported?

options.text: Answer the refund question from the shipping passage.
options.feedback: Similarity alone does not establish policy applicability.

options.text: Look for applicable evidence or explain that this passage is insufficient.
options.feedback: Correct: verify that evidence actually supports the requested claim.

options.text: Always treat the top score as confidence in the answer.
options.feedback: Retrieval scores are not calibrated answer correctness probabilities.

items.explanation: Retrieval ranks candidates. The application must still decide whether those candidates cover the requested entity, policy version, conditions and exception. A plausible passage can be irrelevant or superseded. Do not turn ranking position into an unsupported business conclusion.
hints: Ask which claim the passage can support.

items.title: Defend an idempotent task API
items.scenario: Design a task-acceptance endpoint for clients that may retry after disconnects. Include concurrent requests with the same key and a key reused with a different body.
rubric: Persist operation identity with accepted state.
Reject mismatched bodies for the same key.
Resolve concurrent submissions to one durable result.
items.model_answer: Authenticate before resolving an operation; scope keys to a trusted actor and operation type. Persist a canonical payload hash and task ID atomically under a uniqueness constraint. Return the existing result for a matching retry; reject changed content. Explain expiration, replay after expiry, and an ambiguous downstream side effect. A database row alone does not make a remote system idempotent.
hints: Draw the commit and lost-response boundaries.

items.title: An obsolete response arrives last
items.scenario: Request A starts, then B starts. B finishes, and A responds after its abort was requested. Which rule preserves the right response?

options.text: Always display the last received response.
options.feedback: Arrival order does not establish which user request owns the view.

options.text: Accept a response only when its request generation still owns the active view.
options.feedback: Abort saves work when supported; an ownership/generation check prevents already queued stale responses from overwriting B.

options.text: Use only a loading boolean.
options.feedback: A boolean cannot identify which of several requests completed.

items.explanation: Abort saves work when supported; an ownership/generation check prevents already queued stale responses from overwriting B.
hints: Compare logical request identity with arrival order.

items.title: The answer looks finished but the stream closed
items.scenario: Frames 1, 1 and 2 were received; the duplicate is identical. No terminal event arrives before disconnect. What state is justified?

options.text: Mark Complete because the text ends with a period.
options.feedback: Presentation is not authoritative protocol completion.

options.text: Apply the duplicate once and retain a clearly incomplete result for recovery.
options.feedback: Duplicate-safe presentation and explicit terminal events are separate responsibilities. Reconcile the operation through its own durable identity.

options.text: Dispatch the business action again to recover the stream.
options.feedback: Replay of presentation must not repeat an independently committed effect.

items.explanation: Duplicate-safe presentation and explicit terminal events are separate responsibilities. Reconcile the operation through its own durable identity.
hints: Which event proves completion under this protocol?

items.title: A crash crosses the checkpoint boundary
items.scenario: A document mutation and source checkpoint share one transaction. A fault is injected after the document write but before commit. What must the fixture prove?

options.text: The checkpoint advances but the document is skipped.
options.feedback: This loses source data on restart.

options.text: Neither the projection nor the checkpoint commits; replay safely applies the same event.
options.feedback: An atomic transaction rolls back both local facts. Across independent stores, use idempotency/reconciliation instead of claiming the same atomic boundary.

options.text: The write always survives because its SQL statement finished.
options.feedback: Statement execution is not transaction commit.

items.explanation: An atomic transaction rolls back both local facts. Across independent stores, use idempotency/reconciliation instead of claiming the same atomic boundary.
hints: Distinguish statement completion from durable commit.

items.title: An old event arrives after the watermark
items.scenario: An event timestamped 12:04 arrives at 12:09 after its five-minute window has emitted a result. What is the correct interpretation?

options.text: Assign it to 12:05–12:10 because that is when it arrived.
options.feedback: That changes an event-time metric into an arrival-time metric.

options.text: Use the declared late-data correction/review policy for the original event-time window.
options.feedback: Window assignment, allowed lateness and update/retraction policy belong to the result contract.

options.text: Declare the source impossible because watermarks prove completeness.
options.feedback: A watermark does not eliminate all late or corrected events.

items.explanation: Window assignment, allowed lateness and update/retraction policy belong to the result contract.
hints: Identify the meaning of event time versus processing time.

items.title: Rate limiting meets the token budget
items.scenario: A request has 30 reserved tokens remaining. Each attempt reserves 10 input plus 20 maximum output tokens. The first attempt is rate limited. May a second attempt run under this fixture policy?

options.text: Yes, because a failed attempt cannot consume resources.
options.feedback: The fixture deliberately reserves every attempt conservatively; real provider accounting must be checked.

options.text: No. The first reservation exhausted the local allowance; obtain a new explicit budget decision.
options.feedback: Budget is checked before each attempt. A retryable error does not grant extra resources or permission.

options.text: Retry indefinitely until a valid answer appears.
options.feedback: This violates finite attempt, deadline and spend limits.

items.explanation: Budget is checked before each attempt. A retryable error does not grant extra resources or permission.
hints: Read the stated accounting policy rather than assuming a billing rule.

items.title: Calculate metrics from a failure trace
items.scenario: Gold IDs are {sale, normal}. The first two results are [irrelevant, sale]. Which pair is correct?

options.text: Recall@2 = 1.0; reciprocal rank = 1.0.
options.feedback: Only one of two gold items was recovered and the first relevant hit is rank two.

options.text: Recall@2 = 0.5; reciprocal rank = 0.5.
options.feedback: State the evaluation unit and denominator. Empty-gold queries need a separate answerability/abstention policy.

options.text: Recall@2 = 0.5; reciprocal rank = 0.25.
options.feedback: Reciprocal rank is 1 divided by rank, not rank squared.

items.explanation: State the evaluation unit and denominator. Empty-gold queries need a separate answerability/abstention policy.
hints: Count recovered gold identities and locate the first relevant rank.

items.title: A permitted citation supports the wrong rule
items.scenario: An answer cites a permitted sale-policy source but states an ordinary-return deadline absent from that passage. What follows?

options.text: Accept because the source ID exists.
options.feedback: Existence and scope do not prove semantic support.

options.text: Membership passed, but support/applicability failed; withhold or repair the claim.
options.feedback: Keep source membership, caller scope, applicability and claim support as separate checks.

options.text: Increase the confidence rating to make the answer usable.
options.feedback: A confidence label cannot supply missing evidence.

items.explanation: Keep source membership, caller scope, applicability and claim support as separate checks.
hints: Which fact did source-ID validation actually establish?

items.title: Estimate replicas and defend the assumption
items.scenario: Assume 50 requests/s, 2 s mean occupancy, 4 independent slots/replica and 70% target utilization. What is the planning estimate?

options.text: 25 replicas with a guaranteed p95 under 2 seconds.
options.feedback: That ignores headroom and confuses a mean-capacity relation with a tail guarantee.

options.text: 36 replicas, followed by load validation of the independence and tail-latency assumptions.
options.feedback: ceil(50×2/(4×0.7)) is 36. Real GPU batching, memory and dependencies can invalidate the independent-slot assumption.

options.text: 143 replicas because each slot requires its own replica.
options.feedback: The declared replica has four slots; do not change the units.

items.explanation: ceil(50×2/(4×0.7)) is 36. Real GPU batching, memory and dependencies can invalidate the independent-slot assumption.
hints: Track units through arrival rate × mean time ÷ capacity.

items.title: Higher task quality hides a privacy regression
items.scenario: Baseline quality is 0.90; candidate quality is 0.94 with acceptable latency but one other-tenant disclosure. Should the candidate pass?

options.text: Accept because average quality improved.
options.feedback: An aggregate improvement cannot compensate for the forbidden disclosure.

options.text: Reject it because the critical authorization invariant failed.
options.feedback: Predeclare critical invariants and inspect their failures separately from average quality.

options.text: Hide the failed case from the dataset.
options.feedback: Removing the evidence makes the gate misleading.

items.explanation: Predeclare critical invariants and inspect their failures separately from average quality.
hints: Which requirement is a hard boundary rather than an optimization target?

items.title: A backfill replays a deleted policy
items.scenario: Revision 4 deletes a policy. A delayed revision 2 upsert arrives during a historical backfill. What should the projection do?

options.text: Restore revision 2 because it arrived more recently.
options.feedback: Arrival order is not document revision order.

options.text: Retain the revision-4 tombstone and prevent the old upsert from republishing the document.
options.feedback: Deletion requires version-aware state and reconciliation of derived stores; current access rules must survive rollback/replay.

options.text: Delete only the browser cache.
options.feedback: The stale derived index and backfill can still expose the source.

items.explanation: Deletion requires version-aware state and reconciliation of derived stores; current access rules must survive rollback/replay.
hints: Compare authoritative revision order with processing time.

items.title: A declared type is not a parsed response
items.scenario: An HTTP response is cast with `as Answer` and the compiler passes. A new server returns citations as a string. What protects the UI boundary?

options.text: Trust the cast because TypeScript checked it.
options.feedback: This does not enforce the stated boundary.

options.text: Parse unknown input and validate the runtime shape before publishing state.
options.feedback: Correct: preserves the invariant under the given failure.

options.text: Catch only rendering errors after the value enters state.
options.feedback: This changes presentation or policy without repairing the failure.

items.explanation: A compile-time assertion does not inspect bytes received at runtime. Validate the discriminated union and field limits before treating a body as trusted state.
hints: Identify the authoritative decision and the evidence that actually crosses the boundary.

items.title: The test set became a tuning set
items.scenario: A learner compares ten models using the final test accuracy, changes features after inspecting those test errors, then reports the best value as an unbiased held-out score. What repair is needed?

options.text: Rename the best model and keep the number.
options.feedback: This does not enforce the stated boundary.

options.text: Declare the old test data used for selection and evaluate the frozen decision on a fresh valid holdout.
options.feedback: Correct: preserves the invariant under the given failure.

options.text: Average only the five best scores.
options.feedback: This changes presentation or policy without repairing the failure.

items.explanation: Selecting and engineering against test outcomes consumes that set. Fix the split and preprocessing design, use validation for decisions and reserve a fresh appropriately grouped or timed holdout.
hints: Identify the authoritative decision and the evidence that actually crosses the boundary.

items.title: Package pins do not identify the connection profile
items.scenario: A package lock pins a protocol SDK, but its client automatically falls back to an older supported profile. The app requires a capability absent in that profile. Which gate is missing?

options.text: A check that the package version string looks current.
options.feedback: This does not enforce the stated boundary.

options.text: An assertion of the actual negotiated wire profile and required advertised capability.
options.feedback: Correct: preserves the invariant under the given failure.

options.text: A faster JSON parser.
options.feedback: This changes presentation or policy without repairing the failure.

items.explanation: SDK versions and negotiated wire profiles are separate. Reject unsupported profiles or missing required capabilities rather than silently weakening the contract.
hints: Identify the authoritative decision and the evidence that actually crosses the boundary.

items.title: An accumulating correction is not a fresh delta
items.scenario: Beam emits an accumulating pane totaling 5, then a late-event correction totaling 12. A database sink adds both and shows 17. What is the correct write policy for this fixture?

options.text: Add each pane again after restart to ensure delivery.
options.feedback: This does not enforce the stated boundary.

options.text: Upsert the latest total under a stable owner/window identity and handle replay/version ordering.
options.feedback: Correct: preserves the invariant under the given failure.

options.text: Discard all late events without changing the declared policy.
options.feedback: This changes presentation or policy without repairing the failure.

items.explanation: The corrected accumulating pane already contains the earlier accepted values. Store the authoritative aggregate with appropriate ordering and replay identity; do not add the two cumulative totals.
hints: Identify the authoritative decision and the evidence that actually crosses the boundary.

items.title: A restore resurrected deleted data
items.scenario: A valid backup contains d2. A later authoritative deletion ledger says d2 must stay deleted. After restoring the old backup, when should the deletion be reapplied?

options.text: After users report seeing d2.
options.feedback: This does not enforce the stated boundary.

options.text: Before exposing restored data or rebuilding visible projections.
options.feedback: Correct: preserves the invariant under the given failure.

options.text: Never: backup integrity overrides newer deletion authority.
options.feedback: This changes presentation or policy without repairing the failure.

items.explanation: A valid old snapshot can contain data deleted later. Preserve independent deletion authority and apply it before visibility, including derived indexes and caches.
hints: Identify the authoritative decision and the evidence that actually crosses the boundary.

items.title: Averages cannot grant permission
items.scenario: A candidate improves mean answer quality but a network response now contains another owner’s private source. The release policy requires zero cross-owner disclosures. What is the release decision?

options.text: Ship because average quality improved.
options.feedback: This does not enforce the stated boundary.

options.text: Block release, repair server scope and retain the disclosure as a regression.
options.feedback: Correct: preserves the invariant under the given failure.

options.text: Hide the source link in the browser and ship.
options.feedback: This changes presentation or policy without repairing the failure.

items.explanation: A critical permission invariant is a separate release gate. The unauthorized bytes have already reached the browser; an aggregate score or hidden link cannot repair the disclosure.
hints: Identify the authoritative decision and the evidence that actually crosses the boundary.

items.title: Diagnose a blocked event loop
items.scenario: A FastAPI endpoint executes a synchronous, CPU-intensive Python loop for 500 ms without await. Other async I/O endpoints share that worker's event loop. Which change directly addresses the mechanism while preserving bounded capacity?

options.text: Wrap the CPU loop in create_task() without changing its internals.
options.feedback: create_task schedules a coroutine, but its blocking CPU code still monopolizes the event-loop thread.

options.text: Move the CPU-heavy work to an appropriately bounded process/worker pool and propagate deadlines.
options.feedback: Correct: offloading the CPU work prevents it from blocking that loop; admission and deadlines control overload.

options.text: Increase the browser's fetch timeout to 60 seconds.
options.feedback: Longer patience does not restore event-loop scheduling or prevent queue starvation.

items.explanation: Asyncio is cooperative; a coroutine without a suspension point blocks other tasks sharing its thread. Process/worker isolation can free the event loop, but adds serialization, memory and cancellation/recovery obligations. Test p99 and event-loop lag under concurrent traffic.
hints: Distinguish task scheduling from executing CPU work in parallel.
Identify where control returns to the event loop.

items.title: Reason about queue saturation
items.scenario: In an idealized M/M/1 model with one server at μ=100 requests/second, arrival rate rises from λ=90 to λ=99 requests/second. Which interpretation correctly describes mean time in system, and what should a production team do next?

options.text: Mean time stays 10 ms because each lookup is O(1); only code complexity matters.
options.feedback: Algorithmic O(1) lookup work says nothing about waiting near server saturation.

options.text: Idealized mean grows from 100 ms to 1 second; then measure actual request distributions and percentiles instead of treating the model as a measured p99.
options.feedback: Correct: 1/(μ−λ) yields .1 and 1 seconds under M/M/1 assumptions, not observed production p99.

options.text: Mean increases from 10 ms to 11 ms; use Little's Law to calculate exact p99.
options.feedback: The queueing denominator is remaining capacity (μ−λ), and Little's Law relates averages, not tail percentiles.

items.explanation: The ideal M/M/1 result is 1/(100−90)=0.1 s and 1/(100−99)=1 s. This estimate assumes a stable Poisson/exponential single-server queue. Real LLM-backed workloads require observed p95/p99, queue wait, service-time distributions, cancellations, timeout/error handling and fair admission controls.
hints: Write λ for arrival rate and μ for service capacity.
Evaluate 1/(μ−λ); then distinguish expectations from measured percentiles.
